title: Abstract Class Constructors
summary: Understand why abstract classes have constructors when they cannot be directly instantiated, how super() constructor chaining operates, and best practices for base state initialization.
learningObjectives: Explain the technical rationale for constructors in abstract classes (base state initialization)
Trace constructor execution flow from concrete child up to Object and back down
Identify compilation errors when abstract base classes lack no-arg constructors and child constructors omit super(...)
Avoid the dangerous antipattern of calling overridable methods inside abstract class constructors
expectedOutcomes: You can design robust abstract class constructors that validate and initialize base class invariants
You understand why calling overridden methods inside an abstract constructor leads to null-state bugs

activities.title: Everyday Analogy: The Vehicle Chassis Factory

realWorldMetaphor.scenario: An automotive conglomerate produces a universal truck chassis with steel rails, brake lines, and an axle. You cannot buy just the chassis and drive it on public roads—it has no cabin, steering wheel, or headlights. It is abstract. However, every pickup truck, delivery van, and ambulance built on this platform passes through the chassis assembly station first, stamping a serial number and torquing the axle bolts.
realWorldMetaphor.mapping: The chassis assembly step is the `abstract class constructor`. Even though a bare chassis is never sold to consumers, the constructor must execute first so the subsequent cabin and interior constructors have a solid foundation to build upon.
realWorldMetaphor.takeaway: Abstract constructors exist to prepare and validate foundational state before concrete child constructors add their specialized features.

activities.title: Constructor Execution in Abstract Classes
Constructor Chaining with State Validation
activities.explanation: DatabaseRecord has no default constructor. UserRecord must explicitly call super(recordId). The base constructor executes first to validate and record creation timestamp.

stepByStepWalkthrough.description: `DatabaseRecord` constructor runs, verifying `recordId` is not null or blank and stamping `createdAt`.
Control returns to `UserRecord` constructor to assign `this.email`.
Both parent and child states are guaranteed to be fully initialized.

activities.title: The Leaking 'this' in Constructors Antipattern
activities.explanation: Look closely at the output: when BaseWidget constructor calls render(), label is still NULL! The field initializer label = 'CLICK_ME' has not run yet because parent constructor runs first!

stepByStepWalkthrough.description: `BaseWidget` constructor calls `render()`. Dynamic dispatch routes to `ButtonWidget.render()`.
At this moment, `ButtonWidget` constructor has NOT executed, and field initializers have not run. `label` is default `null`!
`label is: null` is printed, illustrating why overridable method calls in constructors are dangerous.

questions.question: Why does Java permit constructors in abstract classes when abstract classes cannot be directly instantiated?
options: To allow reflection to instantiate them directly
To initialize state and enforce invariants defined in the abstract superclass when concrete subclasses are created
It is an accidental syntax carry-over from C++ with no purpose
Only to define static variables
questions.explanation: Constructors in abstract classes are required to initialize base class state and invariants during subclass constructor chaining (`super()`).

questions.question: What happens if an abstract class declares only a parameterized constructor `public Base(int id) {}` and the child constructor omits `super(...)`?
options: The compiler automatically supplies id = 0
Compilation error: constructor Base in class Base cannot be applied to given types; no default constructor found
The program compiles with a warning and throws NullPointerException at runtime
id is assigned null
questions.explanation: When no no-arg constructor exists in the superclass, the compiler requires child constructors to explicitly invoke `super(...)` on line 1.

questions.question: Can an abstract class constructor be marked `abstract` (e.g. `public abstract MyClass();`)?
options: Yes, if all methods in the class are abstract
No, constructors cannot be abstract in Java
Only in interface constructors
Yes, if marked protected
questions.explanation: Constructors cannot be abstract, static, final, or native in Java. A constructor must have an implementation to initialize state.

questions.question: Why is calling an overridable method inside an abstract class constructor considered a dangerous anti-pattern?
options: It is rejected by the compiler with a syntax error
The subclass constructor and field initializers have not run yet, so the overridden method runs against uninitialized (null/zero) subclass state
It forces the child method to become private
It causes garbage collection to hang
questions.explanation: Parent constructors run before child constructors and field initializers. Invoking an overridden method inside a parent constructor exposes half-initialized child state.

questions.question: If an abstract class has no constructors explicitly written, what does the compiler do?
options: It generates a public default no-arg constructor that calls super() to Object
It forbids subclasses from being created
It makes all fields static
It throws a ClassFormatError
questions.explanation: Just like concrete classes, if no constructor is written, the compiler automatically inserts an implicit default no-arg constructor calling `super()`.

questions.question: Can an abstract class constructor have `protected` access?
options: No, constructors must always be public
Yes, protected is a recommended best practice for abstract class constructors because they are only intended to be called by subclasses
Only in package java.lang
Only if declared final
questions.explanation: `protected` is ideal for abstract class constructors since external classes cannot instantiate them anyway; only extending subclasses need access.

options: B
BA
AB
Compilation error
questions.explanation: `B`'s constructor implicitly calls `super()`. The superclass constructor `A()` executes first ('A'), then `B()` completes ('B'), printing 'AB'.

questions.question: Can an abstract class declare multiple overloaded constructors?
options: No, only one constructor is allowed in abstract classes
Yes, abstract classes can provide multiple overloaded constructors for flexible subclass initialization
Only if all are private
Only if all parameters are Strings
questions.explanation: Abstract classes support full constructor overloading, allowing subclasses to invoke different `super(...)` signatures as needed.

questions.question: Can a subclass constructor call `this(...)` to delegate to another constructor before calling `super(...)`?
options: No, super() must be on line 1 of every constructor
Yes, a constructor can call this(...) on line 1, as long as the chain eventually ends in a constructor that calls super(...)
Only in interface implementations
Only if the superclass is concrete
questions.explanation: Constructor chaining via `this(...)` is legal on line 1. The target constructor in the chain will ultimately call `super(...)` to initialize the abstract parent.

questions.question: What is the primary role of constructor validation (e.g. checking `if (arg == null)`) in an abstract class?
options: To prevent the JVM from allocating memory
To enforce foundational domain invariants once in the superclass so subclasses cannot be created with corrupted base state
To convert checked exceptions to unchecked exceptions
To automatically format strings
questions.explanation: Centralizing validation in the abstract constructor guarantees that all subclasses inherit clean, validated base state without duplicating validation code.

interviewQA.question: Explain the exact execution order when instantiating a subclass of an abstract class in Java.
interviewQA.answer: When `new SubClass()` is called, memory for the unified heap object is allocated and defaulted (zeros/nulls). The subclass constructor is invoked and immediately branches to `super(...)`. This propagates up to `java.lang.Object`. The constructors then execute downwards: `Object()` initializes first, followed by `AbstractSuperClass()` executing its field initializers and constructor body, followed finally by `SubClass()` executing its field initializers and constructor body.

interviewQA.question: Why is it considered dangerous to call an abstract or overridden method from inside an abstract class constructor?
interviewQA.answer: In Java, parent constructors run before child constructors. If an abstract class constructor calls an overridden method, the JVM dispatches the call to the child's implementation before the child's constructor or field initializers have executed. If the child's method accesses any of its own instance variables, it will observe uninitialized default values (null, 0, false), frequently resulting in `NullPointerException` or corrupted state.

interviewQA.question: Why should abstract class constructors typically have `protected` access rather than `public`?
interviewQA.answer: Declaring an abstract class constructor `protected` accurately communicates design intent: the class cannot be directly instantiated from outside the package, and the constructor exists strictly for subclasses to chain into via `super()`. While `public` works because the compiler blocks `new AbstractClass()` anyway, `protected` enforces cleaner API encapsulation.

interviewQA.question: How do you enforce immutability of base fields in an abstract class hierarchy?
interviewQA.answer: You declare the base fields `private final` in the abstract class and require them as parameters in the abstract class constructor. Because they are `final`, they must be assigned during constructor execution and cannot be modified thereafter. Subclasses access them via `public` or `protected` getters, preventing any child from altering the base invariants.

interviewQA.question: Can an abstract class constructor throw checked exceptions? What impact does that have on subclasses?
interviewQA.answer: Yes. If an abstract class constructor declares a checked exception (e.g., `throws IOException`), every subclass constructor that calls `super(...)` MUST also declare that checked exception (or a broader supertype) in its `throws` clause, because constructor calls cannot be caught in a `try-catch` block before `super()` executes.

interviewQA.question: Can an abstract class have a `private` constructor? If so, how can it be subclassed?
interviewQA.answer: Yes. An abstract class can have a `private` constructor. However, external classes cannot extend it because their constructors cannot access `super()`. It can ONLY be subclassed by nested (inner or static nested) classes defined within the same outer class, a pattern often used to build controlled algebraic data types or singleton hierarchies.

activities.title: Self-Evaluation Checklist
checklist: I understand why abstract classes have constructors despite being non-instantiable.
I can trace constructor chaining from subclass up through abstract superclass to Object.
I know why overridable methods must NEVER be called inside an abstract constructor.
I understand how uninitialized child fields cause NullPointerExceptions if called from parent constructors.
I know how to declare `protected` constructors in abstract classes.
I understand compiler errors when a parent lacks a default constructor and `super(...)` is omitted.
I can use `final` fields in an abstract class to enforce immutable base state.
I understand how checked exceptions on abstract constructors impact subclass constructor declarations.
I know how to overload constructors in abstract classes.
I can use constructor parameter validation in abstract classes to protect domain invariants.

practiceProblems.title: Product SKU and Price Constructor Chaining
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Pass product data to an abstract base constructor:

1. Abstract Class AbstractProduct:
   - Fields: protected final String sku, protected double price
   - Constructor: AbstractProduct(String sku, double price) validating price >= 0
   - Concrete Method: public void displayInfo() printing 'SKU: <sku> | Price: $<price>'

2. Class BookProduct (extends AbstractProduct):
   - Constructor: BookProduct(String sku, double price, String author) calling super(sku, price)

Test in Main:
AbstractProduct p = new BookProduct("BK-1001", 19.99, "Joshua Bloch");
Call p.displayInfo();.
hints: In BookProduct constructor, line 1 must be: super(sku, price);
practiceProblems.description: Pass product SKU and price to the abstract product base constructor using super().

practiceProblems.title: Audit Event Logging with Timestamps
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Record security audit events from scratch:

1. Abstract Class AuditEvent:
   - Fields: protected final String eventId, protected final long timestamp
   - Constructor: AuditEvent(String eventId, long timestamp)
   - Abstract Method: public abstract String getDetails();
   - Concrete Method: public void logEvent() printing '[Timestamp: <timestamp>] (<eventId>) ' + getDetails()

2. Class LoginAuditEvent (extends AuditEvent):
   - Fields: private String username, private String ipAddress
   - Constructor: LoginAuditEvent(eventId, ts, user, ip) calling super(eventId, ts)
   - Method: @Override public String getDetails() returning 'User ' + username + ' logged in from ' + ipAddress

Test in Main:
AuditEvent ev = new LoginAuditEvent("EVT-501", 1700000000L, "sarah", "192.168.1.1");
Call ev.logEvent();.
hints: In UserLoginEvent, call super(eventId, timestamp) on the first line.
Implement getDetails() in UserLoginEvent returning formatted user and ip details.
practiceProblems.description: Validate and record audit event IDs and timestamps in an abstract base constructor from scratch.

practiceProblems.title: Immutable Bank Vault Configuration
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Validate configuration in an abstract constructor from scratch:

1. Abstract Class VaultConfig:
   - Fields: protected final String vaultId, protected final int securityLevel
   - Constructor: VaultConfig(String vaultId, int securityLevel) ensuring level is between 1 and 5
   - Abstract Method: public abstract boolean requiresBiometrics();
   - Concrete Method: public void printConfig() printing:
     Vault: <vaultId> | Security Tier: <securityLevel>
     Biometrics required: <requiresBiometrics()>

2. Class HighSecurityVault (extends VaultConfig):
   - Constructor: HighSecurityVault(id, level) calling super(id, level)
   - Method: @Override public boolean requiresBiometrics() returning securityLevel >= 4

Test in Main:
VaultConfig v = new HighSecurityVault("VAULT-ALPHA", 5);
Call v.printConfig();.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Vault: VAULT-ALPHA | Security Tier: 5
Biometrics required: true
hints: HighSecurityVault constructor passes 5 as the default security level to super(vaultId, 5).
practiceProblems.description: Validate vault security tiers (1 to 5) inside the abstract constructor from scratch.

practiceProblems.title: Fix Missing super() in Subclass Constructor
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Fix compiler error: 'constructor MessageService cannot be applied to given types':

Bug: MessageService defines `MessageService(String provider)`. EmailService forgot to call `super(provider)`!

Your Task:
1. In EmailService(String provider, String host), add `super(provider);` as the first line.
2. Implement `send(String msg)` printing '[<provider> @ <host>] ' + msg.

Test in Main:
MessageService svc = new EmailService("SendGrid", "smtp.sendgrid.net");
Call svc.send("Verification code 4492");.
hints: In EmailService constructor, add super(provider); on the very first line.
practiceProblems.description: When an abstract parent defines a constructor with arguments and no default constructor, children MUST call super(arg).

practiceProblems.title: Network Router Multi-Tier Initialization
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build a 3-tier device initialization hierarchy from scratch:

1. Abstract Class HardwareDevice:
   - Field: protected String serialNo
   - Constructor: HardwareDevice(String serialNo) printing '[1] Hardware initialized: ' + serialNo

2. Abstract Class NetworkDevice (extends HardwareDevice):
   - Field: protected String macAddress
   - Constructor: NetworkDevice(serial, mac) calling super(serial) and printing '[2] Network NIC bound: ' + mac

3. Class WifiRouter (extends NetworkDevice):
   - Field: private int antennas
   - Constructor: WifiRouter(serial, mac, antennas) calling super(serial, mac) and printing '[3] Router configured with ' + antennas + ' antennas'
   - Concrete Method: public void startRouter() printing 'Router ' + serialNo + ' (' + macAddress + ') ONLINE'

Test in Main:
WifiRouter router = new WifiRouter("RT-909", "00:1B:44:11:3A:B7", 4);
Call router.startRouter();.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
[1] Hardware initialized: RT-909
[2] Network NIC bound: 00:1B:44:11:3A:B7
[3] Router configured with 4 antennas
Router RT-909 (00:1B:44:11:3A:B7) ONLINE
hints: In NetworkDevice constructor, call super(serialNo) first.
In SmartRouter constructor, call super(serialNo, macAddress) first.
practiceProblems.description: Trace initialization steps up a 3-tier hardware and router hierarchy from scratch.
